title: What science taught
hook: attention, habit and compassion can grow, modestly

segments.voice: Yesterday, a year of thinkers, and your line was four lines. Which of the four did you read twice? This week ran from choosing a practice and its warning signs, through one well and different ends, to closing the schools and opening the year's look back. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-one.

Somewhere in the middle of this year, the path left the old books for the lab. Monks in brain scanners. A gorilla walking unseen through a room of people passing basketballs. Habit curves, urge surfing, people in a hurry passing someone in need. Then a hard turn: the replication crisis, and a long look at which famous findings held up and which didn't. It was a lot of studies. Today asks a simpler question, the kind a friend asks over dinner: so what did science actually teach you? Not the headlines. The modest, honest summary you'd still stand behind.
screen: `FROM THE OLD BOOKS TO THE LAB.` → `WHAT HELD UP, WHAT DIDN'T.` → `THE MODEST SUMMARY.`

segments.voice: Three things, and one word that goes with all of them. First, attention. Attention is limited, and it wanders. The studies this path looked at suggest it can be trained, a little, with practice: returning, again and again, is the exercise. Second, habit. Habits live in cues and places, they form through repetition, and a missed day doesn't erase the curve. The psychologist William James, in his Principles of Psychology, put the whole idea in one sentence: "The great thing, then, in all education, is to make our nervous system our ally instead of our enemy." Repetition is how an ally is made. Third, compassion. The research suggests compassion can be practiced, not only felt, and that practice can shift it somewhat. And the one word for all three: modestly. This year also taught where the claims went too far. Some celebrated results didn't hold up when others tried them again. Some effects were smaller than the headlines. Mindfulness is not a cure-all, and it can be hard for some people. That honesty is part of the lesson, not a footnote to it. So the summary is not "meditation rewires everything." It's quieter, and sturdier. Attention, habit and compassion behave more like muscles than like fixed traits. They respond to steady, ordinary practice, by small amounts, over time. Which means a useful kind of evidence about your own practice is the evidence in your own life: what, this year, actually grew?
screen: `ATTENTION CAN BE TRAINED, A LITTLE.` · `HABIT: MAKE THE NERVES AN ALLY.` · `COMPASSION CAN BE PRACTICED.` · `MODESTLY.` · then, large: `WHAT, THIS YEAR, GREW?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: note what grew in you. Settle, and breathe. Think back to where you were at the start of this year. Then ask three quiet questions. Is your attention any steadier, even a little? Is there one habit that holds now that didn't before? Is there someone you're kinder to? Don't measure. Don't argue with yourself. Just notice one small thing that grew, and let yourself see it. The bell holds the time.
What science taught. Attention, habit and compassion can grow with practice, modestly, and some big claims didn't hold up. Today's word.
Your line: it grew. Today, write down the one thing you noticed, in plain words, with no exaggeration, the way a careful scientist would. Day one thousand four hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Careful researchers who study contemplative practice describe its effects on attention, habit and compassion as real but modest, and call for replication; practitioners who want to track their own change sometimes keep a simple journal.
